autor: William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347), Friar Minor, in exile at the court of Louis the Bavarian in Munich
quelle: Monarchia S. Romani Imperii, sive tractatus de iurisdictione imperiali seu regia et pontificia seu sacerdotali, ed. Melchior Goldast, tom. II (Frankfurt, 1614), pp. 993–1231. Internet Archive, bub_gb_wCH1hULfLpkC (Google scan of the Bibliothèque municipale de Lyon copy). Public domain.
hinweis: Goldast's printing, three centuries older than the critical edition, is the only public-domain text of the work; the critical edition (Guillelmi de Ockham Opera politica I–II, Manchester 1940–1963) is in copyright and is not used. The Latin was transcribed from the page images, with u and v, the ae ligature and the common abbreviations normalized; the words of the bull are kept in Goldast's brackets. Seven excerpts from a work of 124 chapters; cuts are marked […]. The English is this site's working translation (CC0).

sections.blurb: Ockham's answer, written at Munich, to Quia vir reprobus, the pope's reply to Michael of Cesena: the bull quoted phrase by phrase, the objections of Michael's party set against each phrase. Excerpts: the prologue, the definitions of use of fact and of the right of using, the power to appropriate after the fall, Judas's purse, what a pope may change, and the pertinacious heretic.

units.orig: Doctoris gentium & Magistri Beati Pauli irrefragabili authoritate decernitur, omnia esse probanda, id est, ratione discutienda, secundum Glossam. Quinimo iuxta illud Philosophi: Dubitare de singulis, non est inutile. Quia, sicut dicit quidam Sapientum non minimus: Non omne quod verisimile est, statim verum est. Sicut saepius, quod primum incredibile est, videmus non continuo falsum. Crebro siquidem faciem mendacii veritas retinet: crebro mendacium specie veritatis occultatur. Diligenter itaque examinanda sunt omnia & probanda, ne praecipitanter falsa pro veris a nimis credulis approbentur. Tunc autem efficatius examinantur omnia & probantur, exagitataque veritas magis splendescit in lucem, cum pro utraque parte contradictionis fortius & acutius allegatur. Proinde cum multa asserta in constitutione, Quia vir reprobus, (pro quibus in eadem constitutione multiplicius allegatum existit) nonnulli satagant impugnare: ideo ipsorum motiva duxi praesentibus inserenda, ut utriusque partis allegationibus electis, ipsa veritas clarius elucescat. Ut autem apertius dictae constitutionis sciatur intentio, qualiterque contra ipsam obiectiones adversariorum procedant magis appareat. Ne quis dicat, quod verba, non mentem impugnant, tota constitutio per particulas cum reprobationibus est ponenda. Deinde obiectiones & responsiones impugnantium annectentur. Ad subiiciendas vero obiectiones (cum nesciam) minime respondebo. Sed quod constitutionis antedictae conditor respondeat, ardenter affecto.
units.en: By the unimpeachable authority of the teacher of the gentiles and master, blessed Paul, it is decreed that all things are to be proved, that is, according to the Gloss, examined by reason. Indeed, according to the Philosopher's saying, 'to doubt about particular things is not useless'. For, as one not the least of the wise says, 'not everything that is likely is at once true'; just as we often see that what at first seems incredible is not therefore false. For truth often wears the face of a lie, and a lie is often hidden under the appearance of truth. All things, then, are to be examined and proved with care, lest falsehoods be rashly approved as truths by the too credulous. And all things are examined and proved most effectively, and truth, once stirred up, shines out more brightly into the light, when both sides of a contradiction are argued with the greatest force and acuteness. Since, therefore, some are busy attacking many things asserted in the constitution Quia vir reprobus (for which much is argued in that constitution), I have thought it right to insert their reasons here, so that, the arguments of both sides being set out, the truth itself may shine more clearly. And so that the intention of that constitution may be known more openly, and it may appear more plainly how the objections of its adversaries proceed against it, and lest anyone say that they attack the words and not the meaning, the whole constitution is to be set out piece by piece with the rebuttals; then the objections and replies of the attackers will be added. To the objections set out below, however, I shall make no reply at all, since I do not know. But I ardently desire that the author of the said constitution should reply.
units.note: Goldast's heading calls the work 'the Work of Ninety Days, because he completed it in the space of ninety days', and wrongly makes it part of Ockham's Dialogus. It answers Quia vir reprobus (16 November 1329), the pope's reply to Michael of Cesena's appeals of 1328. The prologue sets the form of the whole work: the bull is quoted phrase by phrase, and each phrase is followed by what 'the impugners', Michael's party, say against it; the author claims to report them and to reply to nothing 'since I do not know'. The apostle is 1 Thessalonians 5:21, 'prove all things'; the Philosopher is Aristotle, Categories 7.

units.orig: Dicunt autem, quod quia impugnatus sub multiplicitate vocabulorum errores conatur inducere, & molitur prosternere veritatem, ad evidentiam dicendorum quosdam terminos in hac constitutione saepe usitatos volunt exponere: considerando videlicet, quid sit usus: quid usus facti: quid usus iuris: quid ius utendi: qui sunt simplices usuarii: quae sunt res usu consumptibiles: & quae non sunt usu consumptibiles: quid dominium: quid proprietas: quomodo accipiantur talia vocabula, meum, tuum, suum & huiusmodi. [...] De usu facti dicunt, quod usus facti est actus utendi re aliqua exteriori: sicut inhabitare, comedere, bibere, equitare, vestem induere, & huiusmodi. Hoc per scripturam Divinam & per scientiam legalem, ac etiam per dicta illius impugnati declarant. Dicitur enim, sicut allegatum est superius, Iudicum 19 Habentes panem & vinum in meos, & ancillae tuae usus. Constat autem, quod isti usus erant, comedere panem & bibere vinum. Igitur usus pro actu comedendi, bibendi nonnunquam accipitur.
units.en: They say further that, since the man they attack tries to bring in errors under a multiplicity of words and labours to overthrow the truth, they wish, to make plain what is to be said, to expound certain terms often used in this constitution: considering, namely, what use is; what use of fact is; what use of right is; what the right of using is; who are simple users; which things are consumable by use, and which are not; what ownership is; what property is; how such words as 'mine', 'yours', 'his' and the like are taken. [...] Of use of fact they say that use of fact is the act of using some external thing: such as living in a house, eating, drinking, riding, putting on a garment, and the like. This they show from divine scripture and from the science of law, and also from the words of the man they attack. For it is said, as was cited above, in Judges 19: 'having bread and wine for my use and for your handmaid's'. And it is plain that these uses were eating bread and drinking wine. Therefore use is sometimes taken for the act of eating and drinking.
units.note: Here and throughout, the doctrine is given as what 'they say', the impugners of the pope. The list of terms is the programme of chapter 2, the longest in the work. Ad conditorem had argued that in things consumed by use, an egg, a cheese, a crust of bread, use cannot be separated from ownership (Decr. Conditorem [5]). The answer begins by taking the act of using apart from any right to it: the friars' 'simple use of fact' (Exiit [4]) is eating and drinking, not a legal position.

units.titel: The right of using, and the poor at a rich man's table
units.orig: Quarto exponunt, quid est ius utendi: dicentes, quod ius utendi est potestas licita utendi re extrinseca, qua quis sine culpa sua, & absque causa rationabili privari non debet invitus: & si privatus fuerit, privantem poterit in iudicio convenire. Dicitur (Potestas licita) ad differentiam potestatis illicitae, qua fur saepe utitur rebus alienis. Multi etiam alii frequenter per potestatem illicitam propriis rebus utuntur. (Qua quis sine culpa sua) etiam ponitur ad differentiam gratiae, qua saepe alicui conceditur potestas licita utendi re aliqua, qua tamen ad libitum concedentis (absque enim culpa sua & causa) licite privari potest, solummodo, quia concedens concessam revocat potestatem: sic invitati pauperes a divite, habent licitam potestatem utendi cibis & potibus positis ante se, quos tamen invitans ad placitum suum poterit amovere: & si amoverit, non poterunt invitati propter hoc invitantem in iudicio convenire, nec aliquam actionem habent contra ipsum, & talis potestas saepe vocatur gratia in iure.
units.en: Fourth, they explain what the right of using is, saying that the right of using is a licit power of using an external thing, of which one ought not to be deprived against one's will without fault of one's own and without reasonable cause; and if one has been deprived, one can sue the depriver in court. 'Licit power' is said to distinguish it from illicit power, by which a thief often uses other people's things; many others, too, often use their own things by an illicit power. 'Of which one ought not to be deprived without fault of one's own' is put to distinguish it from grace, by which a licit power of using something is often granted to someone, of which he can nevertheless be licitly deprived at the pleasure of the grantor (that is, without fault or cause of his own) simply because the grantor revokes the power he granted. Thus poor people invited by a rich man have a licit power of using the food and drink set before them, which the host can nevertheless take away at his pleasure; and if he takes it away, the guests cannot sue the host in court on that account, nor have they any action against him; and such a power is often called in law a grace.
units.note: The definition for which the work is remembered in the history of rights: a right is a power one can defend in court. On this account the friars have a licit power of using, but by grace, like guests at a table, revocable at the host's pleasure and without any action at law; so they use without any right, and the pope's argument that a use without right would be an unjust use (Decr. Conditorem [9]) does not reach them.

units.titel: The power to appropriate, after the fall
units.orig: Sed primi parentes vel filii eorum diu post peccatum diviserunt inter se bona temporalia quo ad distincta dominia. Ergo post peccatum habuerunt commune dominium. Sed illud non acquisierunt per peccatum. Ergo ante peccatum habuerunt dominium commune. Ad hoc dicunt isti impugnatores, quod primi parentes post peccatum non habuerunt dominium commune omnium temporalium proprie loquendo de dominio: sed habebant potestatem appropriandi sibi, & etiam acquirendi commune dominium: quia quae in nullius bonis sunt, occupanti conceduntur. Et ideo illa proprietas non fuit proprie dominium commune, sicut nec modo potestas appropriandi seu acquirendi illa, quae caelo terra marique capiuntur, est proprie dominium commune. Quia si esset proprie commune dominium nullus deberet sibi appropriare aliqua ipsorum absque communitatis consensu. Et ideo si concedatur, quod illa potestas appropriandi fuit commune dominium, dicunt isti impugnatores, quod tale dominium non fuisset in statu innocentiae, si primi parentes non peccassent, quia ibi non fuisset potestas appropriandi. Et si quaeratur, unde igitur habuerunt primi parentes talem potestatem appropriandi res temporales, quam non habuerunt ante peccatum? Dicunt isti, quod habuerunt illam potestatem ex natura corrupta, quia ex dictamine rationis naturalis convincitur, quod expedit posse peccantibus, quod etiam habeant potestatem appropriandi sibi aliqua, nisi eorum aliqui eadem potestate sponte se privent, ita quod nullus debet in principio cogi talem potestatem dimittere.
units.en: But the first parents, or their sons, long after the sin divided the temporal goods among themselves into distinct ownerships. Therefore after the sin they had common ownership. But they did not acquire it through sin. Therefore before the sin they had common ownership. To this these impugners say that the first parents after the sin did not have common ownership of all temporal things, speaking properly of ownership, but they had a power of appropriating things to themselves, and also of acquiring common ownership; for things that are in no one's goods are granted to the one who occupies them. And so that property was not properly common ownership, just as now the power of appropriating or acquiring the things that are taken in the sky, on land and at sea is not properly common ownership. For if it were properly common ownership, no one ought to appropriate any of them to himself without the consent of the community. And so, if it is granted that that power of appropriating was common ownership, these impugners say that such ownership would not have existed in the state of innocence, had the first parents not sinned, because there would have been no power of appropriating there. And if it is asked where, then, the first parents got such a power of appropriating temporal things, which they did not have before the sin, they say that they had that power from corrupted nature, because by the dictate of natural reason it is shown to be expedient for those who are able to sin to have also a power of appropriating things to themselves, unless some of them deprive themselves of that power of their own accord; so that no one ought in the beginning to be compelled to give up such a power.
units.note: The pope had argued in Quia vir reprobus that God gave Adam ownership of the earth, so that property was as old as creation and could not be foreign to Christ. The impugners answer that before the fall there was dominion over the creatures but no property; after it, natural reason grants fallen men a power to appropriate, which the Roman law of occupation expresses ('what belongs to no one is granted by natural reason to the one who occupies it'). Property comes after sin, and a friar may renounce the power to acquire it. 'That property' is as printed; the argument requires 'that power'.

units.orig: (Item Iohannes supponit ipsum loculos habuisse) hoc verum est, quantum ad aliqualem dispensationem: sicut etiam multi fratres Cistercienses habent aliqualem dispensationem in rebus, in quibus tamen non habent dominium seu proprietatem (in quibus Iudas quae mittebantur portabat.) Quaeret aliquis, quomodo Christo permittente & consentiente Iudas portabat pecuniam: cum Christus sibi, sicut aliis Apostolis, interdixerit portare pecuniam? Dupliciter dici potest, uno modo, quod Christus, qui erat supra omnem legem positivam, dispensavit cum eo, alio modo, quod haec fecerit tempore necessitatis, quae legem non habet, aliis autem temporibus non portavit. (Loculos habebat Iudas.) Arguat hic ille impugnatus, quod Iudas, non Christus habuit proprietatem loculorum: quia hic dicitur Iudas loculos habuisse. In tota autem sacra Scriptura non invenitur vocaliter dictum, quod Christus habuit loculos, si ergo non obstante, quod dicatur Iudam loculos habuisse, non potest inferri, quod habuit proprietatem in loculis: sequitur quod nec ex scripturis potest inferri, quod Christus habuit proprietatem in loculis. (Habebat Dominus loculos.) Ista sunt verba Augustini, non Evangelistae, quae recte sunt intelligenda, scilicet quod Dominus habebat loculos, scilicet quantum ad aliqualem dispensationem absque dominio & proprietate (tribuebat) hoc est, ordinabat tribuendum.
units.en: ('Likewise John supposes that he had the purse.') This is true as to a certain administration: just as many Cistercian brothers also have a certain administration of things in which they nevertheless have no ownership or property. ('In which Judas carried what was put in.') Someone will ask how, with Christ permitting and consenting, Judas carried money, when Christ had forbidden him, as he had the other apostles, to carry money. It can be answered in two ways: in one way, that Christ, who was above every positive law, dispensed him; in another, that he did this in a time of necessity, which has no law, and at other times did not carry it. ('Judas had the purse.') Let the man they attack argue from this that Judas, not Christ, had the property of the purse, since here it is said that Judas had the purse. In the whole of holy scripture it is nowhere said in words that Christ had a purse; if, then, although Judas is said to have had the purse, it cannot be inferred that he had property in the purse, it follows that neither can it be inferred from scripture that Christ had property in the purse. ('The Lord had a purse.') These are the words of Augustine, not of the evangelist, and they are to be rightly understood: that the Lord had a purse as to a certain administration, without ownership and property. ('He gave out'), that is, he ordered it to be given out.
units.note: John 12:6 and 13:29: Judas 'had the purse' and carried what was put in it; Augustine's gloss 'the Lord had a purse' was the pope's proof text. Nicholas III had explained the purse as Christ's condescension to the weak (Exiit [3]). The words in brackets are the phrases of Quia vir reprobus, quoted piece by piece and answered one by one, as the prologue announced. 'Necessity has no law' is a maxim of canon law.

units.orig: [quin contra ordinata per summos pontifices circa talia liceat successoribus aliquid ordinare] Dicunt isti, quod summi pontifices neque de paupertate Christi & apostolorum eius, neque de rebus quas habuerunt, neque de simplici usu facti ipsorum aliquid unquam ordinaverunt, sed veritatem de praedictis docuerunt, & ipsam esse tenendam diffinierunt & ideo non licuit isti nec ordinando nec diffiniendo nec docendo aliquid contrarium penitus attentare. quia licet multa ordinata per summos pontifices, quae Fratres Minores servare tenentur, possit Romanus pontifex mutare: de vita tamen Christi & apostolorum eius nihil potest penitus mutare, nec licet sibi aliter docere de vita eorum, quod sancti patres hactenus docuerunt. [quod Nicolaus tertius praefatus expresse in sua declaratione inseruit, ut superius plenius continetur] nusquam legitur, quod Nicolaus tertius unquam aliter docuerit vel diffinierit de vita Christi & apostolorum eius, quam praedecessores sui.
units.en: ['... that it is lawful for successors to ordain something against what the supreme pontiffs have ordained about such matters.'] They say that the supreme pontiffs never ordained anything about the poverty of Christ and his apostles, nor about the things they had, nor about their simple use of fact, but taught the truth about these things and defined that it was to be held; and so it was not lawful for this man to attempt anything at all to the contrary, whether by ordaining, defining or teaching. For although the Roman pontiff can change many things ordained by the supreme pontiffs which the Friars Minor are bound to observe, he can change nothing at all about the life of Christ and his apostles, nor is he allowed to teach about their life otherwise than the holy fathers have taught until now. ['Which the said Nicholas III expressly inserted in his declaration, as is contained more fully above.'] It is nowhere read that Nicholas III ever taught or defined about the life of Christ and his apostles otherwise than his predecessors.
units.note: The distinction of the appeal of Sachsenhausen between the key of knowledge and the key of power (Sachs. Poverty [5]), in Ockham's terms: a pope may change the order's regulations, which are ordinances, but not what his predecessors taught about Christ's life, which is doctrine. The pope's position was the reverse: Nicholas III had ordained, and 'it belongs to the maker of the canons' to revoke what does harm (Decr. Conditorem [1]).

units.titel: A heretic only if he will not be corrected
units.orig: Finito tractatu hic conclusio totius constitutionis subiungitur. In hac enim parte impugnatus ostendit, quare constitutionem fecerit ante dictam, ac qualiter ipsam duxerit promulgandam. Sed isti impugnatores cum in parte praecedenti, ut asserunt, sufficienter probaverint, istam constitutionem esse haereticalem, hic per verba praemissa volunt aperte ostendere, quod conditor constitutionis eiusdem est pertinax & haereticus reputandus. Saepe enim doctrina alicuius est haeretica censenda, quamvis auctor eiusdem inter haereticos sit minime computandus. Ad cuius evidentiam dicunt esse sciendum: quod si quis erraverit circa veritatem catholicam, quam credere explicite non tenetur: si paratus est corrigi, non est haereticus reputandus. sed si non est paratus corrigi, pertinax & haereticus est censendus. unde August. ut habetur 24. q. 3. ca. dixit apostolus, ait: qui sententiam suam quamvis falsam ac perversam nulla pertinaciter animositate defendunt, praesertim quam non audacia suae praesumptionis pepererunt, sed a seductis atque in errorem lapsis parentibus acceperunt, quaerunt autem cauta sollicitudine veritatem, corrigi parati cum invenerint, nequaquam sunt inter haereticos deputandi.
units.en: The treatise finished, here the conclusion of the whole constitution is added. In this part the man they attack shows why he made the said constitution and how he thought fit to promulgate it. But these impugners, having sufficiently proved in the preceding part, as they assert, that this constitution is heretical, want here, through the words set out above, to show openly that the maker of that constitution is to be held pertinacious and a heretic. For often someone's teaching is to be judged heretical although its author is by no means to be counted among the heretics. To make this plain, they say it must be understood that if someone has erred about a catholic truth which he is not bound to believe explicitly, then if he is ready to be corrected he is not to be held a heretic; but if he is not ready to be corrected, he is to be judged pertinacious and a heretic. Hence Augustine says, as is found in C. 24 q. 3 c. Dixit apostolus: 'Those who defend their opinion, however false and perverse, with no pertinacious animosity, especially an opinion they did not give birth to by the boldness of their own presumption but received from parents who were seduced and had fallen into error, and who seek the truth with careful anxiety, ready to be corrected when they find it, are by no means to be reckoned among heretics.'
units.note: The last chapter. Quia vir reprobus ends, at the head of this page, 'Given at Avignon, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the ninth year of our pontificate'. The bull is of 16 November 1329, the fourteenth year of John XXII; Goldast's 'anno 9' is a misprint. The line between a heretical teaching and a heretical person, with pertinacity as the mark of the heretic, is the ground on which Ockham built his later case that a pope who will not be corrected is no pope. The inquisitor at Toulouse had used the same test on the Beguins he handed to the secular arm: they persisted 'pertinaciously' (Sent. Hospitalis [4]). Goldast's running head on this page wrongly reads 'Compendium errorum papae'; the text is still the Opus nonaginta dierum.
